author: Kierkegaard
title: Abraham told four ways
where: *Fear and Trembling*: the Preparation, the Panegyric on Abraham and the Preliminary Expectoration, in the English of L. M. Hollander (1923)
about: Kierkegaard published this book in Copenhagen in 1843 under the name Johannes de silentio, John of silence. Its subject is Genesis 22, where God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. The first passage comes from four paragraphs on weaning a child, one after each of four retellings of the story. The second comes early in a speech in praise of Abraham, and in the third the narrator, who says he cannot understand Abraham, imagines meeting a man of the same faith in the Copenhagen of his day.

view.says: Auden cites Bonhoeffer, who died a martyr: an earthly happiness that God grants should simply be accepted. Kierkegaard could not truthfully have claimed as much for himself, Auden writes, but his Knight of Faith, who is drawn in this book, shows he knew this was a defect in him and no virtue. Kierkegaard, he says, holds such a man to be what everyone ought to be and admits he cannot understand him.
view.quote: The ideal Christian he describes is happily married, looks like a cheerful grocer, and is respected by his neighbors.
view.source: “A Knight of Doleful Countenance” (1968), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 192

lenses.label: Refrain
lenses.name: refrain
lenses.plain: words that come back at a set place in a song or poem; here, in the paragraph after each of four tellings, the same opening and a matching last sentence
lenses.caption: Kierkegaard tells Abraham’s journey four times, and after each telling comes a paragraph about a mother weaning her child. Three of these open on the same seven words, and the second adds has grown and. All four close on a sentence that begins Happy and says who: three times he who, once the child who. In a song, a phrase that returns at a set place is a refrain, and the book’s subtitle is Dialectical Lyric. The returning paragraph marks each telling as one of a set. The narrator says so: a man thought about the event in these and in many similar ways, and always ended by asking who can understand Abraham.
lenses.why: After each of four retellings of Abraham’s journey comes a paragraph on weaning a child, opened and closed alike: a refrain that marks each telling as one of a set, which is how the narrator describes them.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the same openings and closes in the Danish. What a refrain is: the Online Etymology Dictionary and Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5, where it belongs to a stanza; the word is used here of prose. The subtitle, *Dialektisk Lyrik*: the title page of 1843. The narrator’s account of the four tellings: the [last paragraph of the Preparation](#/read/kierkegaard/p2:18).

lenses.label: Turn

ties.say: The verb of the opening comes back, with *worse means* beside it: worse than blackening a breast. The Danish is stronger: *more dreadful means*.
Here the one called happy is the child, who has lost a mother only in the sense just given.
The mother’s sorrow at the parting comes back as a sorrow someone was spared.
Nearly the same words, and the same tense.

lenses.caption: Each last sentence takes up a word of its own paragraph: wean, mother, sorrow, stronger food. The paragraphs say what a mother does, as a rule. Three last sentences turn to the past: needed not, lost not, needed not. A past tense speaks of a case that is over, and each of the three says what someone was spared: worse means, any other loss of a mother, more sorrow. The fourth alone stays in the present and has no not.
lenses.why: The paragraphs say what a mother does as a rule; three last sentences turn to the past, a case that is over, and each says what someone was spared: worse means, another loss, more sorrow.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage: the repeated words and the tenses, the same in Kierkegaard’s Danish. *More dreadful*: Ferrall and Repp’s dictionary of 1845, under *Forfærdelig*. What each of the three says someone was spared: the last sentences themselves.

lenses.label: Tellings
lenses.what: Genesis 22 and the four tellings: what Abraham does in each, how each ends, and the paragraph on weaning that follows

facts.Abraham: says that he and the boy will come back, tells Isaac that God will provide the lamb, and takes the knife
facts.the end: an angel stops him; a ram is offered, Abraham is blessed, and they go home

facts.Abraham: blesses and comforts Isaac, who begs for his life; then turns wild, says he is an idolater and that this is his own wish and not God’s command
facts.the end: Isaac calls on God as his only father; Abraham thanks God: better the boy think him inhuman than lose his faith
facts.called happy: the one who needed no worse means to wean the child

facts.Abraham: rides with his eyes on the ground, binds Isaac and draws the knife without a word, then sees the ram and offers it
facts.the end: home; Abraham grows old and is never happy again; Isaac thrives as before
facts.the mother: hides her breast, and the child no longer has a mother
facts.called happy: the child who lost its mother in no other way

facts.Abraham: rides lost in thought about Hagar and her son, driven out by him; he draws the knife
facts.the end: he rides back alone, again and again, to ask pardon for having been willing; he finds no rest
facts.the mother: sorrows with the child at the parting
facts.called happy: the one who kept the child near and had no more sorrow

facts.Abraham: makes everything ready calmly; as he turns aside for the knife his left hand clenches in despair and he trembles, and Isaac sees it
facts.the end: home; Isaac has lost his faith, and no one ever speaks of it
facts.the mother: has stronger food ready, so that the child will not die
facts.called happy: the one who has the stronger food ready

lenses.caption: The four tellings open on the same six words, the early morning of Genesis 22:3, and all four add Sarah, whom that chapter never names. Each changes Abraham. He lies to save Isaac’s faith; he obeys and never has joy again; he begs pardon for having been willing; his despair is seen. In Genesis 22 his son is spared and he is blessed. No telling ends in a blessing. The tellings are one man’s thoughts, and the Preparation opens with him: he admired the story more with age and found it less and less clear.
lenses.why: The tellings keep the Bible’s opening and change Abraham, and none ends in a blessing, as Genesis does; the Preparation gives them as the thoughts of a man who found the story less and less clear.
lenses.stands: The four tellings read beside Genesis 22 in the King James Bible. The notes of the Danish edition, *Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter*, vol. K4, say that the tellings paraphrase Genesis freely and that Sarah is not in that chapter. The man who thinks them: the [opening](#/read/kierkegaard/p2:0) and the [close](#/read/kierkegaard/p2:18) of the Preparation.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: Genesis 21:8 tells how Isaac grew and was weaned, and how Abraham gave a feast that day. The Danish edition has found no source for the mother who blackens her breast.
A maiden is an unmarried girl. The next sentence gives the result: the child no longer has a mother.
A Danish dictionary of 1845 gives *Held* as good luck, fortune, success. Where the English Bible has *blessed* at Luke 23:29, the Danish New Testament of 1819 has another word, *salige*.
The Danish *den, der* is he or she who, and the Danish says *the child* where Hollander says *his child*.

lenses.caption: Happy is Held in the Danish: good luck, good fortune. Each last sentence calls someone lucky. Kierkegaard’s book has this cry five times: four times here, and once in the Preliminary Expectoration, of whoever can make the movements of faith. There the translator, L. M. Hollander, writes Blessed. Hollander’s he and his child say more than the Danish den, der and Barnet: the one who, the child. The Danish leaves open whether a woman or a man is called lucky. Genesis gives Isaac’s own weaning a single verse, one chapter before the sacrifice.
lenses.why: Happy translates a Danish word for good luck, cried five times in the book, the fifth of whoever can make the movements of faith; where Hollander says he, the Danish leaves open whether a woman or a man is meant.
lenses.stands: *Held*, *den* and *der*: J. S. Ferrall and T. G. Repp, *A Danish-English Dictionary* (1845). The five places where the Danish has *Held*: a count on the text of *Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter*, vol. 4; the fifth is in the [Preliminary Expectoration](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:15). Isaac’s weaning: Genesis 21:8, in the King James Bible. That no source is known for the blackened breast: the notes of the same edition; *maiden*: the Online Etymology Dictionary.

lenses.label: Build
lenses.caption: Two sentences run on one plan. First come others who were great, two in the first sentence and four in the second. Then but turns to one who is greater than all of them. The first time that one is he who believed in God. The second time the place holds a name, Abraham, which the speech has not yet said. Before the name comes, the paragraph that ends here gives this verdict five times, each time to an unnamed he who. The school pattern for a speech of praise compares its subject with someone else, to raise the praise. This speech builds the top rank first, so the name arrives already defined.
lenses.why: Two sentences keep one plan, others who were great and then one greater than all, and the second puts the name Abraham where the first had he who believed in God: the name arrives already defined.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. That this is the first *Abraham* in the speech, and the sixth time the paragraph gives its verdict: counted in the text printed here, from [the head of the speech](#/read/kierkegaard/p3:0). The Danish holds the name back to the same sentence. The comparison in a speech of praise: *Silva Rhetoricae*, on the encomium.

lenses.label: Paradox
lenses.name: paradox
lenses.plain: a statement that contradicts itself on the surface and is still meant as true; here, four times, a ground of greatness defined by a word of blame
lenses.caption: The second sentence names four things heroes are great by: strength, wisdom, hopes, love. Then it gives Abraham the same four in the same order, each defined by a word of blame: weakness, folly, madness, hatred of one’s self. Each of the four is a paradox, and the book later uses the word of Abraham: his life, the narrator says, has the enormous paradox for its content.
lenses.why: The four things heroes are great by are given to Abraham, each defined by a word of blame: four paradoxes, for a man whose life the narrator calls a paradox.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Paradox as *Silva Rhetoricae* and the Online Etymology Dictionary define it. The narrator on the paradox of Abraham’s life: the [Preliminary Expectoration](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:7).

lenses.label: Sources

notes.note: Paul asks to be spared a suffering and is told that strength is made perfect in weakness. The Danish edition says the phrase probably points here.
Paul: whoever seems wise in this world must become a fool to be wise, for this world’s wisdom is foolishness with God. The edition calls the phrase an allusion to this.

notes.gloss: no source in the Danish edition
notes.note: The edition has no note here. Where this translation has *expression*, the Danish has *Form*, that is, form. The close of the speech says Abraham found the expression for the divine madness, where the edition points to Plato’s *Phaedrus*.
The verse says that whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for life eternal. The edition says the phrase perhaps alludes to it.

lenses.caption: The notes of the Danish edition trace three of the four pairings to the New Testament. Strength and weakness: probably Paul, whose Lord tells him that strength is made perfect in weakness. Wisdom and folly: Paul again, for whom this world’s wisdom is foolishness with God. Love and hatred of one’s self: perhaps John, where he who hates his life in this world keeps it. For hope and madness the notes give nothing. So the orator’s sentence praises Abraham, three times in four, in terms the notes trace to Paul and John.
lenses.why: By the Danish edition’s notes, three of the four pairings point to Paul and John, so the orator’s sentence praises Abraham largely in the New Testament’s terms.
lenses.stands: The notes to this sentence in *Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter*, vol. K4, with their *probably* and *perhaps*. The verses in the King James Bible: 2 Corinthians 12:9, 1 Corinthians 3:18–19, John 12:25. The divine madness: the [close of the speech](#/read/kierkegaard/p3:17).

lenses.label: Speech
lenses.what: the speech in praise of Abraham, paragraph by paragraph: how long each is and how often it names him

facts.about: the hero, and the poet who can only admire him
the poet as the hero’s memory
the great ranked by what they loved, hoped for and strove with; the name comes in the last sentence
his faith is for this life
what he would have done had he doubted
he does not pray to be spared
the morning, the mountain, the knife
if he had doubted on the mountain
the speaker turns to Abraham and asks his pardon

lenses.caption: In this translation the speech has eighteen paragraphs and 3,375 words. The first two never say Abraham. They are about the poet, who cannot do a hero’s deeds and can only admire and remember. The third ranks the great, and its last sentence is the first to name Abraham, 749 words in. Every later paragraph names him, fifty more times. The school pattern for such a speech runs: introduction, origins and upbringing, deeds, a comparison that lifts the subject, a closing exhortation or prayer. Kierkegaard’s comparison comes early, ahead of the life and of the name, so the name arrives at the top of a ranking already built.
lenses.why: The speech keeps its hero’s name back through 749 words on the poet and on greatness, and sets the comparison ahead of the life, so that Abraham arrives at the top of a ranking already built.
lenses.stands: Words and namings counted in the text printed here, in Hollander’s paragraphs; a naming is the word *Abraham*, possessives included. The Danish also holds the name back to this sentence. The order of a speech of praise: *Silva Rhetoricae*, on the encomium. What the paragraphs are about: the [speech itself](#/read/kierkegaard/p3:0), to its [last paragraph](#/read/kierkegaard/p3:17).

lenses.label: Yet
lenses.caption: Three statements give what anyone could see: the pipe, a likeness to the green-grocer, the unconcern of an idler. Then and yet turns to what cannot be seen: the price of his leisure, the absurd, the movement of infinity. Yet comes four times, as dog does in the Danish, and before the last the narrator breaks in: he could be furious, if only from envy. The paragraphs before say that no outward sign betrays the man. So the look comes first, and what it does not show comes after yet. Auden’s summary of this portrait keeps both halves, the ideal Christian and the cheerful grocer, and adds that Kierkegaard finds the man incomprehensible.
lenses.why: The portrait has shown a man whom no outward sign betrays, so the sentence sets the visible first and brings in what he does after yet, said four times; Auden’s summary keeps both halves.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The four *dog* of the Danish sentence: *Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter*, vol. 4, p. 135. That nothing betrays the man: the [paragraphs before](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:17), and the narrator on what he himself cannot do, [a little later](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:28). Auden’s summary: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 192.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: The Danish edition explains *Spekhøker* as a small tradesman in pork, butter and other provisions, and a dictionary of 1845 gives *chandler, cheesemonger*. A greengrocer sells vegetables. Auden says *grocer*.
The Danish says he buys the opportune time at the dearest price. The edition points to Ephesians 5:15-16, which the Danish New Testament of 1819 words the same way. To redeem is to buy back.
A term of the book. Six paragraphs on, it says the absurd is no category of the understanding and is not the improbable, the unforeseen or the unexpected.
The next sentence explains it: he has resigned everything and then taken hold of it all again. The book calls the first step *infinite resignation* and says faith must pass through it.

lenses.caption: Two kinds of word meet here. From the street: pipe, green-grocer, happy-go-lucky fellow. From the book’s own stock: the absurd, the movement of infinity. Between them stands a phrase of the Danish New Testament: purchases his leisure is, in the Danish, buys the opportune time, as in Ephesians 5:16. The sentence needs both kinds, since it says of one man what the street sees and what the book claims. In lines this translation leaves out just after, Kierkegaard names what this knight of faith alone can do: express the sublime in the pedestrian. The Expectoration of the section’s title is properly a coughing up from the chest, and figuratively a pouring out of the heart.
lenses.why: The sentence says of one man what the street sees and what the book claims, so street words and abstract terms stand together; a few lines on, the Danish says only this knight can express the sublime in the pedestrian.
lenses.stands: *Spekhøker*, *Expectoration*, the phrase from Ephesians and *the sublime in the pedestrian*: the Danish text and notes in *Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter*, vols. 4 (pp. 135–36) and K4, with Ferrall and Repp’s dictionary of 1845. Ephesians 5:16 in the King James Bible; *greengrocer* and *redeem* in the Online Etymology Dictionary. The book on the absurd: [six paragraphs on](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:27). Auden’s word *grocer*: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 192.

lenses.label: Day
lenses.what: the knight of faith’s portrait in this translation’s five paragraphs: when, and whom he is likened to

facts.he: is introduced to the narrator, who starts back

facts.when: at his business; then Sunday, at church
facts.he: treads the ground firmly, is exact at his business, sings in the congregation
facts.likened to: a citizen in his best, off to the park on Sunday; a philistine; a bookkeeping clerk

facts.he: walks out to the forest and home again, thinking of a hot dish his wife may have ready
facts.likened to: a shopkeeper on an outing; a mail-carrier, by his gait; a chef, by his talk; Esau, by his appetite

facts.he: plans a building with a stranger at a building lot
leans in his window, watches the square, smokes his pipe
facts.likened to: a girl of sixteen, for peace of mind; the green-grocer across the street; a happy-go-lucky fellow

lenses.caption: The portrait reaches the window by way of a Sunday: church, an afternoon walk to the forest, home toward evening, the window at dusk. The narrator likens the man to twelve figures, from a parish beadle at first sight to the green-grocer and the happy-go-lucky fellow at the window. He has said why: those who have faith look like the philistines, and he watches in vain for a sign of the infinite. Only at the window does he say what the man does every moment.
lenses.why: The portrait follows a Sunday and likens the man twelve times to someone else because, as the narrator says, those who have faith look like the philistines; only at the window does he say what the man does.
lenses.stands: The portrait itself, from the narrator’s [warning about the philistines](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:15) and its [first paragraph](#/read/kierkegaard/p4:17) to the window: the times of day it names, and the twelve figures the man is likened to by name, counted in the text printed here (a general phrase about worldly people is not counted).

auden.says: In 1947, in his introduction to Baudelaire’s *Intimate Journals*, Auden wrote that the Old Testament has its own idea of the hero, which orthodox Christianity works out more consciously. His example is Abraham, whom poetry would not count a hero, since he has no gifts out of the ordinary. Auden sets him beside Agamemnon, who gives up his daughter for the army of the Greeks and suffers for it. Abraham, by contrast, is told to give up his son to try his faith. He tells no one and obeys, and so the son is spared and a blessing follows. The passage does not name this book.
auden.quote: What makes him exceptional is that he, outwardly an average man, is called by God to an exceptional task and obeys.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 309–10

auden.says: On the same page as his sentence about the cheerful grocer, Auden writes that Kierkegaard’s mastery of his own language shows even through translation: he commands every style, lofty or homely, abstract or concrete. His one great fault as a writer, which Auden finds common in lonely men of genius, is that he does not know where to end.
auden.source: “A Knight of Doleful Countenance” (1968), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 192

auden.says: Introducing a selection of Kierkegaard in 1952, Auden wrote that his pages are often those of a poet or a philosopher, and that he was neither. He was a preacher, whose work was to set out and defend Christian teaching and Christian conduct. Auden compares him with Newman: both had to preach to a society that had turned secular and still called itself Christian.
Reviewing a translation of *Either/Or* in 1944, Auden advised a Christian reader to begin Kierkegaard with this book or with *Training in Christianity*.
auden.source: “A Preface to Kierkegaard,” *The New Republic*, 15 May 1944, in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 213–14

auden.says: Donald Pearce, a student in the class, wrote his notes just after the lectures, since note-taking in class was forbidden. By his account, on a Thursday late in October 1941 Auden described the aesthetic and the ethical attitudes, said that Kierkegaard treats these categories in full, and called him the last of Europe’s great thinkers on ethics. His scheme, as Pearce gives it: ethics gives up the individual for the universal, aesthetics does the reverse, and religion makes the individual a martyr. Religion, he said, is where the other two meet. What was seen of these pages does not name this book.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 129–31 and 134

auden.says: Kenneth Millar, who took the class in the fall of 1941 and later wrote novels as Ross Macdonald, kept notes on it. Michael Kreyling reports that his fullest notes were on this book and on Kafka’s *The Castle*.
auden.source: Michael Kreyling, *The Novels of Ross Macdonald* (2005), pp. 39–40

auden.says: The grocer of Auden’s sentence of 1968 is already in a poem of 1940. Edward Mendelson finds that the sonnets of “The Quest” vary themes of Kierkegaard. In one, “The Hero,” the man who has succeeded in his quest wins little respect, since to other people he seems too much a grocer, and all that sets him apart from people who have run no such risk is the pleasure he takes in small things and in routine. Mendelson sets him beside the knight of faith, whom one would take for a shopkeeper.
auden.source: “The Hero,” in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (1945), pp. 259–60; Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 459–60

auden.says: Two more poems of these years use the book, by Mendelson’s account. “In Sickness and in Health” (1940) calls the command to rejoice absurd because Kierkegaard’s Abraham believed by virtue of the absurd. The idea of two lines of “At the Grave of Henry James” (1941), about dancing lightly, comes from the book’s description of the knights of infinite resignation as dancers. That description stands just after the third passage here, in lines this translation leaves out.
auden.source: Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 476 and 485

sources: The text: Søren Kierkegaard, *Fear and Trembling*, as selected and translated by L. M. Hollander in *Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard* (University of Texas Bulletin no. 2326, 1923), as Project Gutenberg prints it (no. 60333). A note of Hollander’s calls his selection about a third of the book; counted in words against the Danish it is about a quarter.

The Danish: *Frygt og Bæven* (Copenhagen, 1843), in *Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter*, vol. 4 (Copenhagen: Søren Kierkegaard Forskningscenteret, 1997), pp. 99–210 (what is used here stands on pp. 99–136), with the notes to it in vol. K4 (1998), both at tekster.kb.dk.
The King James Bible: Genesis 21:8 and 22:1–19; Luke 23:29; John 12:25; 1 Corinthians 3:18–19; 2 Corinthians 12:9–10; Ephesians 5:15–16.
J. S. Ferrall and Thorleifur Gudmundsson Repp, *A Danish-English Dictionary* (Copenhagen: Gyldendal, 1845): Beleilig, Den, Der, Forfærdelig, Held, Spekhøker.
W. H. Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973): “Søren Kierkegaard” (1952), p. 168; “A Knight of Doleful Countenance” (1968), p. 192.

W. H. Auden, introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), and “A Preface to Kierkegaard” (*The New Republic*, 15 May 1944), in *Prose*, vol. II: 1939–1948, edited by Edward Mendelson (2002), pp. 309–10 and 213–14. Not seen in full.
W. H. Auden, *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (1945): “The Quest: A Sonnet Sequence,” the sonnet “The Hero,” pp. 259–60.

Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 129–31 and 134: notes made after Auden’s lecture of October 1941. Pages 129–30 not seen in full.
Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 459–60, 476 and 485.
Michael Kreyling, *The Novels of Ross Macdonald* (2005), pp. 39–40. Not seen in full.
Online Etymology Dictionary: chandler, greengrocer, maiden, paradox, redeem, refrain.
*Silva Rhetoricae* (rhetoric.byu.edu): paradox, anaphora, and the school exercise of the encomium.
Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification* (1922), chapter 5 and the glossary, on repetition and the refrain.
caveats: The English is L. M. Hollander’s selection of 1923: about a quarter of the book (he says a third). It leaves out the three Problems and much else, and trims the speech in praise of Abraham. Counts and paragraphs follow his text. Which translation Auden’s class read was not found.

Auden’s sentences of 1947 and 1944 were read only in search snippets of the volume reprinting them; those of 1947 do not name this book. His lecture of October 1941 is known from notes a student, Donald Pearce, wrote afterward; what was seen of them does not name it either.

The second and fourth paragraphs on weaning are shown whole; the marks of omission there only divide opening from close. The first and third are shown without their middles. Hollander’s *he* and *his child* say more than the Danish, which has *the one who* and *the child*.
The count of twelve likenesses in the portrait takes each named figure once and leaves out one general phrase about worldly people.

The New Testament sources for the second passage are those proposed in the notes of the Danish edition, which says *probably* of one and *perhaps* of another. *The sublime in the pedestrian* is this page’s word-for-word English for Kierkegaard’s Danish, in lines the translation printed here leaves out.
